items.title: Luxury living and the ultra-rich - When money is no object | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Sell a penthouse for 12 million euros? Build a luxury villa with an infinity pool? Just another average working day in the lives of Mira van der Zalm and Jürgen Willen: They design and sell luxury properties.

Discretion is paramount here. "German clients tend to be rather reserved when it comes to luxury, whereas foreign clients like to show off what they have," says Jürgen Willen - and he knows what he's talking about. On almost every continent, the architect and his team design luxury villas and interiors for a clientele seeking something truly unique. From bathtubs to car lifts with washing facilities, if it's on the wish-list and can be done, Willen will make it happen.
Mira van der Zalm's client base is equally discerning. The estate agent arranges the sale of houses and flats not advertised on the open market - that takes a special level of service. For example, she calls in Jürgen Willen to an Art Nouveau villa in Wiesbaden to check whether it's possible to install an underground parking lot and a spa - and if it can be done in accordance with listed building regulations.

items.title: Our parents are scrolling their lives away | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>When your aging parents can’t put down their phones, where does care end and control begin?

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

In this episode, Vox reporter and producer Miles Bryan talks with internet culture reporter Jessica Lucas about the older adults who are getting hooked on AI-generated videos, and their grown children who are trying to intervene. Her reporting follows families navigating sleepless nights, health misinformation, subscription traps, and an uncomfortable reversal: the parents who may have once warned their kids about screen time as children, now need help managing their own.

They explore how grief and loneliness can draw people into endless scrolling, who profits from keeping them there, and what researchers can (and can’t) tell us about the effects on the aging brain. They also consider the ethical questions facing families who secretly change passwords, curate feeds, or install restrictions. How do you protect someone without taking away their independence, or the online connections that still bring them joy?

Was it holy revelation, shamanic trance, or brilliantly engineered theatre designed to absolve rulers and enrich priests? Follow the clues, feel the heat, and decide for yourself.

items.title: Creatine, debunked
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Creatine is everywhere right now. But are the claims around this classic supplement actually based in real science? Or are they just more marketing hype?

For decades, creatine has been sold to fitness buffs, as a way to build more muscle, faster. Now it’s being pitched to almost everyone, with influencers, podcasters and celebrity doctors claiming it can sharpen your mind, lift your mood, offset sleep deprivation, and even reverse the effects of Alzheimer’s disease. And these wellness claims are driving a real surge in profit — US sales topped half a billion dollars in 2025. 

So what is creatine actually doing in your body? Will it really help you build muscle, or are those dramatic before-and-after photos telling a different story? And when it comes to your brain, is there real evidence behind the claims about memory, mood, and Alzheimer’s, or is the hype getting ahead of the science?

We dug into the research on creatine, from the muscles to the mind, and spoke with exercise scientist Nick Tiller and associate professor Matthew Taylor, whose team at the University of Kansas studied creatine’s effects on people with Alzheimer’s disease.

In Helsinki, there is a public playground where children learn how computers work. A six-metre tower you climb into as a data packet and slide out as output. A flowchart hopscotch where you jump through conditional statements. A binary abacus you move with your whole body.

Linda Liukas designed this playground. Some computational ideas translated into physical space beautifully. Others fell apart the moment they had to survive a four-year-old. items.title: The unicorn - In pursuit of magic | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For centuries, the unicorn has roamed through cultural history, myths and fairy tales. It's been a symbol of healing, destruction - even queer identity. How has this fantastical creature so captured our imaginations?

Legend has it that ever since ancient times, the unicorn has lived in hiding. If it reveals itself at all, it's only ever for a moment - and only ever from a distance. One of the world's most famous mythical creatures, it's been galloping across our cultural histories for centuries. It appears in works of art, on coats of arms and altars, at fountains, on buildings and everyday objects. It appears in fantasy films, has become a symbol of queer identity and an icon of pop culture.

The myth of the unicorn can be traced back to the second millennium B.C. Only quite late in history did it become clear the creature existed in fact only in our imaginations - and yet our fascination with it has never died.

Over time, it's been attributed with countless meanings. It's been thought of as both healing and destructive, wild and untamable, while still serving as a symbol of purity and innocence. And it has always been associated with a deep longing - after someone caught a glimpse of one, they could supposedly never forget it.

But - has anyone ever really seen a unicorn? Where did the idea of a horse with a horn growing from its forehead first come from? How has an animal that has never existed been able to awaken such powerful, true yearning in us for thousands of years? The hunt for its tracks is on...
